transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-12-17 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~49 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Miles (Redwood AE), Priya Anand (Redwood SE), Liam Cho (Redwood SE), Evan Park (CTO - Cobalt), Maria Lopez (ML Eng Lead), Samir Patel (Platform Eng), Nina Roberts (Security)

--- Auto Summary (auto-generated) ---
Jordan gave a walkthrough of Redwood Catalog and Optimize suggestions; Priya dove into the benchmark CSV, compatibility matrix, and kernel mapping notes. Actionable next steps were captured: share raw bench CSV, propose pilot scope, schedule infra sizing.

--- Topics ---
- How catalog shortlists models for LLM chat + RAG
- How to read throughput / p99 latency columns in benches
- Mapping compatibility matrix to quantization and kernel availability
- Deployment pathways (hosted / dedicated / private) and compliance implications

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you carving out time. We're gonna run through a quick catalog handoff plus performance mapping demo — show you how we'd pick a couple of open models, how benches look, and what that means for hosted vs dedicated or private deployments.

[00:16] Evan: Sounds good. Maria and I are mostly focused on cost and p99 latency under load, Samir is here for infra constraints and Nina will ask about compliance.

[00:27] Jordan: Perfect. Priya, want to take the first few slides on the catalog?

[00:30] Priya: Yeah, sure. So the Redwood Catalog groups models by capability and runtime fit — we have a small shortlist for chat+RAG here, you can see variants that are quant-compatible, and we attach bench summaries to each candidate. Quick note — sometimes the auto transcriber calls our product "Redwood Cata Log" on the export, sorry.

[00:52] Maria: Quick question, does the catalog surface the tokenization differences? We've had issues before where tokenization changed effective latency and cost.

[01:03] Priya: Good call. We include tokenizer size and typical prefix length distributions in the metadata — it's in the bench CSV. For example model A here shows longer tokenized prompts for our legal domain corpus which increases effective token count by ~8-12%.

[01:22] Liam: I'm pulling up the compatibility matrix tab — this is important: rows are models, columns are runtime targets (A100 fp16, A100-qa8, H100, CPU-int8 experiments), and then indicators for KV-cache support and optimized attention kernels.

[01:40] Samir: When you say "optimized attention kernels" is that a vendor kernel or Redwood's runtime selection? We run mixed cloud GPUs and on-prem A100s.

[01:52] Priya: It's runtime-level selection. Redwood's compilation layer picks kernels based on arch and seq-len distribution; if a kernel isn't available we fallback to a generic path which costs more cycles. The matrix marks those fallbacks.

[02:10] Jordan: Let's look at a practical example — model X-3B (open) versus model Y-7B. I want to point out the bench for X-3B: 1000 tokens throughput at 200 QPS baseline, p50 ~ 22ms p99 ~ 180ms on our A100 fp16 config. Y-7B is heavier but quantizes better, gives better cost per token under bursty workloads.

[02:42] Maria: Do you have the raw traces? We need to validate p99 tail under our 95th percentile request patterns.

[02:50] Priya: Yes — Jordan will share the raw bench CSV with per-request latencies and hardware labels. You'll see p50/p90/p99 columns and the sample size. Note: some of the sample names got messed up during capture, e.g., "A100-q8" appears as "A100q eight" in the auto text.

[03:15] Evan: One thing to flag — any model that uses large KV cache will balloon memory usage for long conversations. How do you represent that in the matrix?

[03:26] Liam: We have a KV column that estimates peak KV memory per 1k token cache and a scaling multiplier for per-conversation state. For chat-heavy usage we recommend models with KV-compact encodings or using our prefix-cache instead.

[03:42] Maria: On cost: do the benches include batching and continuous batching effects? Our traffic is a mix of single-shot and batched requests.

[03:50] Priya: All our benches run three workload patterns: single-shot, steady-state batching, and burst with continous-batch re-batching. The cost-estimator in Optimize uses those to suggest batch sizes and warm-cache strategies.

[04:04] Samir: For private deployment, what's the process to replicate these benches on our infra? We can't send production data.

[04:12] Priya: We recommend a synthetic workload that mirrors your payload sizes — we can provide a bench harness and scripts. The bench harness outputs the same CSV format so you can drop it into the catalog and get a direct compatibility score.

[04:29] Jordan: I'm going to demo the console now — open to the Models > Shortlist. See here we created a shortlist called "Cobalt-chat-pick" with three candidates.

[04:40] Jordan: (screen share) You'll notice color-coded flags: green for kernels available, yellow for quantization caveats, red for fallback-only paths. Clicking the bench icon opens the raw CSV.

[04:56] Maria: That bench for candidate 2 — the p99 spikes look correlated to sequence length. Is that visible in the CSV?

[05:04] Priya: Yes, the CSV has a sequence_length column; the bench viewer can group by seq len and show latency percentiles per group. It helped one customer discover a prompt-engineering opportunity to trim context windows.

[05:21] Evan: How reliable are the A/B-style rollouts between model variants? We need automatic fallback to a smaller variant if latency SLOs are violated.

[05:31] Liam: Rollouts are built into the runtime — you can define policies like latency threshold triggers, and Redwood will route to a backup model or downgrade quantization level. There's also a canary percent and auto-roll back.

[05:48] Nina: From a compliance perspective, when using Dedicated or Private, do you get separate audit logs and key management?

[05:56] Jordan: Yes — Dedicated gives you tenant-level logs and Private gives customer-controlled KMS and audit trails. We support SAML SSO, RBAC, and integration with Cloud HSM. We'll share SOC2 and ISO artifacts.

[06:10] Nina: Great. Please include the retention policy options and whether logs can be forwarded to our SIEM.

[06:16] Jordan: Will do.

[06:19] Priya: Switching back to bench interpretation — here's a little formula we use for cost-per-request: tokens * per_token_cost + compute_occupancy*time_slot_cost. It factors caching and batching. The Optimize tab will simulate monthly token volume to give you a $/1M token figure under different batch/warm-cache assumptions.

[06:44] Maria: Can we run the Optimize sim with our real monthly distribution? I can upload a histogram.

[06:49] Jordan: Yes, you can upload histograms of sequence length and QPS. We'll run a simulated month and produce recommended batch sizes, quant profiles, and estimated savings.

[06:58] Evan: Let's focus on one concrete candidate — model Z-lite (6B open). Why would we pick it vs X-3B?

[07:07] Priya: Z-lite trades a bit of raw accuracy for better quantization and kernel support; for your RAG use case where many tokens are embeddings and retrieval steps, the throughput wins can matter. Example: on H100 int8-style profiles, Z-lite had 25% lower cost per token in our bench.
transcript_continued:
[07:32] Samir: Any known quirks with Z-lite and KV eviction? We run long sessions and don't want memory creeping up.

[07:40] Liam: The matrix flagged a subtle KV leak in an older conversion of Z-lite; current catalog entry only includes the patched build. We'll note the exact commit.

[07:50] Maria: You mentioned tokenization earlier. How do we compare cross-model tokenization efficiency?

[07:56] Priya: CSV includes avg_token_per_prompt and avg_token_per_response from our sample corpus. For legal text the delta can be material.

[08:10] Jordan: I'm now opening the compatibility scoring view — it's a condensed score combining raw bench perf, kernel availability, quant-compat, and predicted cost. Scores are relative. You can weight criteria — e.g., weight latency higher than cost for interactive SLOs.

[08:28] Evan: Can we export that weighted scoring? Our procurement team wants a simple table.

[08:33] Jordan: Yes, export as CSV or JSON. The JSON has metadata tags you can import to your tracker.

[08:40] Samir: On the topic of procurement, what about reserved capacity for Dedicated? We often need guaranteed throughput during close-of-day batch processing.

[08:50] Jordan: Dedicated has reserved pools and optional burst capacity. We can set SLOs for sustained throughput and a billing model with commit tiers. We'll include sample pricing in the deck.

[09:02] Maria: Can you show an example of Optimize suggesting a quantization change and the downstream accuracy delta?

[09:10] Priya: Sure — here's model Y-7B with fp16 vs qa8. On this classification eval the accuracy drop was 0.8% absolute but cost dropped 40%. We tie those deltas to your eval set so you see real impact.

[09:28] Evan: What does the eval integration look like? Could we run our regulatory QA prompt set?

[09:34] Priya: Absolutely. You can upload evals and annotate golden outputs. The system will run the eval across shortlists and produce regression alerts. We also support prompt-level fail reasons.

[09:46] Nina: Is the eval data stored in Redwood? We need it to remain customer-controlled for Private.

[09:53] Jordan: For Private deployments, evals live in your cluster and we don't retain copies. For Hosted, data retention is configurable and we can limit storage. We'll detail this in the security packet.

[10:06] Maria: Moving back to the bench— I see a weird spike at 2:11 in candidate 1. What caused that?

[10:12] Priya: That was a transient I/O stall on the run host; bench harness marks host-level anomalies. We exclude those or flag them depending on your acceptance criteria.

[10:23] Liam: Also worth noting the bench harness can inject your request distribution. If you want to reproduce, run the harness with your payloads and hardware labels and results will be comparable.

[10:36] Evan: Ok let's talk pilot success criteria. What would Redwood suggest for a minimal viable pilot?

[10:44] Jordan: Typical pilot: 2 models shortlisted, benched on your infra or ours, integrated with your RAG pipeline, 2-week traffic test with 95th percentile latency target < 300ms, and accuracy guardrails defined on your eval set.

[10:58] Maria: We want a cost estimate for 100k monthly active users doing 3 queries per day — can you ballpark during the pilot?

[11:07] Priya: We can run the Optimize sim with that profile and return a $/month estimate. We'll need your histogram and expected concurrency.

[11:16] Samir: For private deployment we need to know estimated GPU hours — how granular is your sizing calculator?

[11:23] Liam: It gives GPU-hour estimates per model for given QPS and SLO target, plus a headroom factor. For long-running stateful chats we suggest a headroom of 25-40% depending on eviction policies.

[11:36] Maria: One more technical: how do you handle multi-region fallbacks? We need data residency in EU for a subset of inquiries.

[11:44] Jordan: Smart routing can pin requests by geo and failover to another region with masking. For EU-only regulated data you can use Private or Dedicated in-region. We'll include region-specific notes.

[11:58] Evan: Anything on cost-accuracy trade-offs for embedding vs generative? Our RAG pipeline depends heavily on embeddings for retrieval.

[12:06] Priya: Embedding ops are cheaper and often run on CPU or cheaper GPU infra; we recommend an embeddings-only pool and a separate generation pool. Optimize can recommend hybrid routing to minimize cost.

[12:20] Nina: From a security checklist perspective, we'll need SSO, audit logs, SOC2 docs, pen test summary, and data residency guarantees.

[12:29] Jordan: Noted — we'll attach those to the follow-up package.

[12:33] Maria: Show me again how we tag models for the pilot and lock a model version.

[12:38] Priya: In the console you can pin a model version on a route; version pin prevents auto-upgrades. We also support canary weights and automatic rollback triggers based on latency or regression to eval.

[12:53] Evan: A lot of this looks great. For the pilot timeline, we're targeting Q1 rollout and need procurement and security review done by end of year.

[13:03] Jordan: We'll prioritize the security packet and pilot proposal so you can start procurement.

[13:08] Liam: Quick note — some of the console labels here are internal names; we'll clean up for your tenant and ensure they match your naming conventions.

[13:15] Maria: Who should I send the eval corpus to? Is there a secure upload?

[13:20] Priya: We'll give you a secure S3 presigned upload for Hosted or instructions for secure transfer for Private.

[13:27] Nina: Can you confirm that the bench CSV redacts any PII by default?

[13:33] Priya: Bench harness can strip PII and hash tokens; by default the demo data is synthetic. We'll provide configuration for redaction.

[13:44] Evan: Ok thanks — can we do a short demo of a failure case and auto fallback?

[13:49] Jordan: Sure — I'll trigger a latency threshold in the console. (pause) Ok, threshold tripped, you can see traffic shifting to the backup model and the route health shows degraded then recovered.

[14:10] Samir: Does that failover keep session continuity or do we lose KV state?

[14:16] Liam: If you failover across model families you likely won't preserve KV cache. We recommend session-level fallbacks in the same model family or design app-level session stitching.

[14:29] Maria: This is helpful. One last question on license: are there any restrictions on derived model artifacts after quantization?

[14:37] Jordan: License depends on model source — for community-licensed models we follow upstream restrictions. For quantized artifacts we provide guidance but licensing is on a case-by-case basis. We'll flag each candidate's license in the catalog entry.

[14:50] Evan: Cool. Let's recap next steps.

[14:53] Jordan: Recap: Jordan to share bench CSV and pricing; Priya to propose pilot scope and acceptance criteria; Samir to send infra topology; Nina to list compliance docs. We'll schedule a private-deploy sizing call next week.

[15:06] Maria: That works. Thanks everyone.

[15:09] Jordan: Thanks all — we'll follow up via email and link in the CRM.

--- End of meeting — 49 minutes recorded (approx) ---
